projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Nathan Kanter was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Nathan Kanter. Mr. Kanter served in the U.S. Army with the 556th AAA Gun Battalion and the 31st General Hospital. He served in the Pacific Theatre, and his highest rank was T-4. I'm Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Kanter's home in Cleveland, Ohio, on December 5, 2002. Nate was 80 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: '41 I was going to school. I was living in Cleveland. I guess you would call it the, the inner city now, in the Glenville area. It was off 125th Street, between Arlington and 125th, in that area.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were going to school; were you in college or --

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: No, I was a senior. I graduated January '41.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. So what were you doing late in '41, on December 7th in particular?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I was working -- I think I was working at a grocery store making like $15 a week, which at that time was the norm, and then I remember it was a Sunday and we had heard on the radio that Pearl Harbor had been bombed. We didn't realize the full extent of what that meant until the next day, of course, when Roosevelt came on and said that this is a day that will live in infamy, and we realized we were going to war.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you know where Pearl Harbor was?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Well, I knew -- I hadn't really been too aware of it, but I knew where Hawaii was, but specifically not Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was your reaction after you heard the president's speech and you knew we were in the war?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I really felt that I'd be getting into service, and I sort of -- I was looking forward to it, frankly, compared to these days.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right, right, exactly. So I assume you were drafted then a little bit later on?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I had gone for my, what you call it, physical, the induction physical, back in January of '42. Not -- no, it was December '42. It was the last week in December, and I guess I passed. I came home, and I had some kind of a stomachache. Next morning, called the doctor, found out I had appendicitis. Went to the hospital, spent New Year's Eve in the hospital. I was supposed to be drafted in January. Called the draft board, told them I just had an operation and I didn't think I would be able to go just then. They said, All right, we're going to give you a little leave and you let us know when you think you're ready, and in March, I said, okay, I'm ready. And I went.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. And you -- which branch?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Army, Army.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you went into the Army?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Allrighty.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I should -- I don't know if I should tell this, but I sort of cheated on the induction exam.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How did you do that?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Well, I was standing in line behind the guy reading the eye chart, and I knew, wearing glasses, I wasn't going to be able to read that eye chart too well, so with my glasses I could read the line that was 20/20, and when they told me to take off my glasses, they said, Read the lowest line you can, and I read that line, not that I could see it, but I read it, so they said, Okay, fine. And I've often wondered, if I could read that without my glasses, what do I need glasses? But anyway, and then they checked my blood pressure and they said, Your blood pressure is high. How serious are you about wanting to get in? I said, I really want to get into the military. They said, All right, we're going to let you lie down for a while. I guess they let me lie down for about 10, 15 minutes, they checked it again, and I passed, and that's how I got in, and I never regretted it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember the day you left then?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Yeah. I remember I left from Hites Lee Road in Mayfield and we went by streetcar then, went down to the induction center at the Standard building, and they swore us in. I guess they took us to lunch, and then we left for Camp Perry.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Left from the terminal tower, I assume?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So did your family see you off or did they see you off at the --

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Actually, no, no, a friend I had then, a girlfriend saw me off, and that was about the only person, really.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right. So what can you tell me about your time in training?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: It wasn't as difficult as I thought it might be. It wasn't too easy either, and I was training for anti-aircraft. I was a truck operator and a power plant operator which operated the range centers, and I understood then that there was an opportunity to get into this Army Specialized Training Program, and you had to have a certain grade on your general classification test, which I had exceeded, and I got orders to report to the Citadel for the Army Specialized Training Program, and I spent six months at the Citadel, and as I was saying, they cut back on the program and they had various exams to see if you could qualify for this pre-med program, and you had to qualify on the exams, you had to go before a board, I can't remember -- I think it was a civilian board, and you had to pass that board to see if they would authorize you to go to the pre-med program, which I did, and I wound up at Johns Hopkins for nine months in beautiful Baltimore.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the intent of the Army Specialized Training Program?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Well, they wanted specialized personnel to handle various aspects of the military. One I may have mentioned was translation, to translate foreign documents, etc., and engineering, basic engineering, you know, to help build bridges, etc., that they might need, so it was taking the people that they felt could adapt themselves to this versus the regular individual who came in as an infantryman or whatever.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It sounds like those jobs were still important. Why -- why, exactly, do you think they discontinued the program? Just the need for manpower?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Manpower, economics. I guess one thing, the universities were very -- very disturbed about that because that's where their student body was coming from, and of course, the military was paying for this. When I got to Hopkins, they had 17-year-olds and people who were 4-F, that was the student body, so when they got all these other people in, you know, that helped build them up. Of course, the Citadel was only cadets plus we soldiers.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you spent nine months at Hopkins?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What were you doing there, exactly?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Taking courses at the college level. I had not been to college before I went in the military, so this was a great opportunity for me. The problem was there were many college students who were in the program. In fact, there were even college graduates, and you're competing with these individuals, so naturally, as they're so used to this and getting the good grades, you got to really work at it, so for nine months I was able to get by, but I was not accepted for med school and then went back into the regular troops.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And what outfit did you go with then?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I went with a medical group. I trained as a first aid person, and I fully expected to have to use this in Japan, but I was in California in '45, it was August '45, we were out in Fort Mason, getting our general orientation, etc., and decide -- learning about when we might be shipping out, and they said an atomic bomb had dropped on Hiroshima. We didn't know what an atomic bomb was, but in my chemistry courses at Hopkins, I had learned that you couldn't split an atom. Evidently they did. But we cheered because we knew that this was the end. And a couple weeks later, they shipped me out to the Philippines instead of Japan.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me about your time in the Philippines then.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I was with the 31st General Hospital, admissions clerk. I did -- it's hard to remember because, you know, it was well over 50 years ago. See, '45, that's about 57 years ago, and I registered the incoming patients and basically general hospital admission work.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Yeah. None of whom I have been able to contact since, but generally you always wind up with two or three guys you pal around with, so it's not -- it's not a place for a person who wants to be alone because you're in the dorm or a tent with 30 other guys, and so you wind up with some good friends.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things did you do for entertainment?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Well, you went to these USO dances. In Baltimore they had a neighborhood home that had converted its basement into a dance place, and on Saturday night, we would go -- several of us would go there and spend Saturday night dancing and so on, and the USO's were always available, so you went to movies, of course. It was not too bad.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, getting back to before they dropped the bomb, were you fairly certain that you were going to be part of the invasion of Japan?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: There was nothing really certain, but the general tenor of our training in California was there was no other reason to be training, and we all assumed that we would be going to Japan.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you doing some kind of specific training that you knew about?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Well, specific training was as a medical technician, you know, as a first aid, as a corpsman, to handle any battle casualties and things of that nature, broken bones and wounds and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: And we got quite extensive training in that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you could just tell because of the way the war was progressing that that would be the next step?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Well, that was the only step left, of course.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Because this was after VE-Day.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Which was I think May?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: May.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: And I wound up in the -- in California, I think it was around May or June, something like that, so there was only one place left and that, of course, was Japan.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did the guys with you feel about that?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: What? About the bomb or --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The fear -- before the bomb.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: You know, actually, you just talked about it, but you don't -- you don't say -- you don't say anything about being afraid or anything, I mean. Look, you're a soldier, you went in, you're expected to do various things, and they tell you this is what you're going to do, and you do it, and of course, it's possible when you got there you were afraid, but up until then, you really didn't give it that much thought.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you know back then about the fanaticism of the Japanese? I mean, we've heard --

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Oh, yeah, we knew quite a bit. We saw movies, you know. Remember the movies were always showing them fighting to the last man and not giving up until they were burned out or killed, so we -- we -- we had heard that they would fight to the last person, and they expected a great number of casualties, and of course, you never thought about that or you tried not to think about that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything specifically about celebrating on VJ-day when you knew it was finally over?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Well, I think we went to a USO dance and everybody was happy and excited. Of course, they were much more excited in New York, but California was the shipping-out place for these South Pacific areas, and I think they were a bit more subdued, but everybody was really happy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Backtracking a bit, do you remember the day FDR died?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I know we were put on special alert. We were told to be much more alert when we were guarding the various posts. I don't know what they expected, but there was much more -- much more intent, and we were much more serious about what we were doing. Of course, everybody was shocked. I mean, nobody had realized at that time that he was really that ill.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They had managed to keep that from most people?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Evidently they had. We knew -- I knew he had polio. I don't think that was hidden, but to know that he was that close to dying, we didn't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction among the guys you were with?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I think everybody was sort of shocked at, what, the president had just died? Sort of disbelief, but when Truman took over, I mean, hardly anybody knew who Truman was, although we knew he had been an officer in World War I.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: But turned out he -- turned out to be quite a president.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there confidence in Truman or did -- was there just a bit of uncertainty?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: At that point no one really knew for sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: From what we had heard, he had very little communication with Roosevelt. He was a vice president, quote, as vice presidents usually are, and from what I had heard, he had very little contact, and we figured, well, whatever will be, will be, as they say.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember mail call, getting letters from home, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. That was -- everybody always looked forward to that, and I used to get not much mail, but I used to get enough mail to keep me happy, and I'd reply, and I'd keep a record of who had sent me mail and who I replied to.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You let them know later that they hadn't written you?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Well, depending on how many days had gone by.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, when you were able to -- being stateside, you were able to write. Were there any real restrictions on what you could write?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Actually, not until I think we got to California. Nobody was censoring the mail that I was aware of, and I think when we got to California they might have been more strict, but other than that, I wasn't aware of any real censorship.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were there any -- very early into the war, thinking of, you know, December '41, January of '42, was there any doubt that we would win?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I don't think anybody ever doubted it, no. Nobody knew how long the war would last, but other than -- I don't think there was any doubt the U.S. would win. After all, we were the most powerful country.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right, and the situation didn't look bleak even after France fell, and, well, that was before that, but even though Hitler had --

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Well, we knew eventually -- we knew eventually we'd have to go in there, and I remember I was at Hopkins on June 6th, D-Day, and everybody was very elated that the invasion had finally started because we figured that it wouldn't be long now and it was going to be over.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Very good. Any -- when you think about that whole experience in the service, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: One does; when I almost drowned.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How did that happen?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: We -- on the way to the Philippines, we stopped at Hawaii, and they gave us a chance to get off the boat and go to the shore, and as I was sitting by the shore, I see a number of people, number of G.I.'s, like about a quarter of a mile out in water up to their hips, and I'm not a swimmer, and I figured, boy, that looks like fun, you know, you're way out there, the water is only up to here. I'm going out there. I started walking. I think maybe about a hundred feet or two hundred feet I suddenly submerged. Evidently they had dug a trench or something and it was way over my head, and fortunately, I came back up, facing shore, and I'm yelling, Help! And there's some guy standing there, not too far away from me, and I realized I better help myself, so I held my breath as much as I could and started paddling underwater. When my breath gave out, my feet touched ground, and I got up, gasping and coughing, and I said to the guy, Didn't you hear me yell for help? He said, I can't swim. I got to the beach and I laid down and I got such a horrible sunburn, that Hawaii sun, but that's how close I came, because I realized had I not hit ground, I don't know if they ever would have missed me or not. That was -- that was the most chilling experience I had.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Obviously you were in the military, but you were on the home front during a lot of the war. Can you tell me anything about the shortages or rationing or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Yeah, I remember the ration cards, four gallons of gas a week, and going to the stores and using your points to get meat or whatever, but I'll tell you, they kept us in good condition. You didn't over-eat, that was for sure, and when I went in, I was 160 pounds. I won't tell you what I am now, but I was in very good condition.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, would the military, would their ration cards be better if they went off-base, tried to buy things? Could you get more meat, whatever?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: It depended on where you were. When I was in Texas, you could go in a restaurant and get meat. And I don't remember -- I don't think you had to have a card as long as you were in uniform, but other cities were different. Evidently Texas had a lot of steer, so it wasn't quite as bad there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But these restaurants, a civilian couldn't necessarily get meat unless they had the card for it?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I, you know, I don't remember because I didn't go to restaurants much as a civilian.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: And I can't recall the meat -- I wasn't much of a meat-eater anyway then, I don't think, and I didn't pay that much attention to it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else? Any particular shortages that you had to deal with?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Not that I can think of at the moment.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were probably better taken care of in the military anyway then.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Yeah, but I don't -- I don't know that the civilians had that difficult a time. I remember coming home on furlough. Of course, you had to have the points.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Yeah. So you didn't get as much maybe as you would have wanted, but I don't think anybody was starving. You make do with what you have.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, very good. Anything else that comes to mind?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Well, I remember when I was discharged, Camp Atterbury, they had two desks; one for immediate discharge, and one for those who wanted to stay in and join the Reserve.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: And I don't know how many of us were there at one time, maybe -- could have been as much as a hundred, and about 90 went to the one desk and ten of us went to the other desk, so I stayed in the Reserve, and I put in my 20 good years, and I got a commission, and I retired, retired as a major, and I draw retirement pay, and I'm part of this TRICARE For Life medical assistance, so I can say that the military has been very kind to me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you called to active duty any time after that?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I had just received a second lieutenant's commission during the Korean War, and I got a phone call and they said, We understand you're a clerk-typist and we think we would like to get you back into active duty, and I said, Well, you know, I just got a commission as a second lieutenant, and the person who called said, Well, then, I guess we can't really use you, and that's as close as I came.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you didn't have to --

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: So I didn't go in on active duty.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But stayed in the Reserve?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Stayed in the Reserve, yeah, and could have been called, because I was in the Active Reserve, the Ready Reserve, but it never became that -- never happened.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I guess I don't know exactly how that works, this being the Reserves. Did you go out on training once in a while or --

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: We would go to two weeks active duty.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How often? Once a year or --

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Once a year. Occasionally you could go twice a year, if you wanted, and then you would go to -- I joined the military government group here and we met once a week. You got points -- you got points -- you got points for going to the meeting. You got points for your active duty, and you had to get 50 points a year to get a good retirement year, so with your 14 days active duty and your 36 meetings or whatever, you would be able to get your 50 points. There were times when I -- one year I got 48 points and a couple years I got like in the 30's, and I thought, jeez, I've lost these years, so I put in much more than 20 to get the really 20 good years. {Coughs} Excuse me. But once you got that 20, all those other years counted.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: So what I thought I had lost was really part of my retirement plan.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So even the years that were less than 50 points, they would include those as part of your --

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Once you got your good --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Once you got your --

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Once you got your 20 good ones.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And you had to get 50 -- 50 points for at least 20 years to get those --

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Right, right, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Interesting.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: And you could get points through correspondence courses.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: So it wasn't that difficult to get them. It was just that you had to, you know, keep your -- keep your mind on it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: And of course most of us were married and had children, so it became a little more difficult to get that two weeks off, and fortunately I was working for the government, so I could get the two weeks off with paid leave, so that worked out pretty well.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you finally retire then?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you had to do --

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I went in in '43, so I had actually 31 years of --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Of active and Reserve?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Of active and Reserve, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, very good. I think that covers it.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Like I said, nothing --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Unless you can think of anything else?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Nothing special or --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, I've never talked to anybody about the specifics of the Reserve. I've talked to guys that were in the Reserve, but I didn't know how that worked. I guess it's similar -- well, it's sort of like the National Guard, right?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I'm not familiar with the National Guard.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You have to do a certain amount of training in the National Guard every year, right?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I wouldn't --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Obviously I've never been in it.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I'll tell you one incident that I found very interesting. I had to have a quadrennial exam, physical exam, in order to maintain my standing in the Reserve, and I think it was 1970 -- when was Vietnam?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That would have been '70 it was going on.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: So I went down to the Standard building for my exam, and there were a bunch of young kids, I guess 18, 19 or whatever, and as we stood in line, and they were there for physicals, the officer said, Anybody who has a doctor's permit or some other document that says you're not eligible for induction, please step forward, and practically the whole line stepped forward, and these were young kids, and I thought, Where are they all getting these permits or statements, young kids, that they don't have to go to Vietnam because they're physically unfit?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Those were all doctor's excuses, you think, at that time? They weren't college deferments or whatever?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I thought they were physical deferments.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. Well, because this was physical exams. Not the same, was it?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: It was -- back in World War II, you know, nobody wanted to be a 4-F. {Coughs} Excuse me. You want to help yourself to anything?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, no, I'm okay. I had -- I just -- three or four cups of coffee and --

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: All of a sudden my throat got dry.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I've had that happening to me for the last few months where I'll talk a little bit and just start coughing.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Well, I don't know how much of this is worth bothering about.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, no, it's interesting, and it's all part of the project.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I mean, that's interesting when you have, obviously my generation, they were working at staying out of the military, but I didn't have to do that. I had a high draft number, so they didn't take me, so I didn't have to make any decisions.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: But when you see all these young kids, all with some kind of physical problem.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: friend of the family who is a doctor or something, who knows. Wow. Sheesh.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: But I passed my physical.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You passed your physical. So you had, so, what, four times a year you had to do that, huh?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: No, every four years.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Every four years, oh, I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Quadrennial.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Quadrennial, every four years, not ---

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: And then every seven years --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Not quarterly.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: -- every seven years you were up for promotion to retain your standing in the Reserves, and the reason I retired, I had the standing to be considered for lieutenant colonel, and in order to do that, you had to have two years of command general staff course, you had to have this, you had to have that. It became much more difficult, and I thought, you know, now is a good time. It was, what, '74? I was already 52, and I thought, about time to drop out, so I had a choice: Resign or retire.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What's the difference?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Resign you get nothing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: So I retired.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So is it just a matter of paperwork? I mean, after --

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: It's a matter of if you resign, you're out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: You retire, you still retain your grade, of course, and you're a retired officer.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So in theory they could call you up again then or what?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: At my age, probably not.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But I mean they -- first couple of years, for instance.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: I don't think so. Once you're retired, I think --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So why wouldn't more guys just retire?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Because they didn't put in the number of years.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Because you have to have the right number of years to actually retire?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Of course.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So they should have put in the years.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Some of my friends, you know, I often asked them Why didn't you stay in the Reserve? Oh, no, I didn't want any part of the military. I took my chances.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They just didn't want to hassle with the whole thing?

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Well, they didn't want to -- once they got out, they wanted out, but once I got out, I thought, you know, it wasn't that bad, so I stayed in, and I'm glad I did.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, I think some guys just got so fed up they just didn't want to see another uniform. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Well, I hope this is of some value.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Nathan Kanter
sp.p: Some use.
